hints: Focus on the type of intermolecular force each compound can make, alkanes only have induced dipole forces while OH and SH groups add polarity.
Compare compounds 1 and 4 first, both are $C_4H_{10}$ alkanes but 1 is branched and 4 is a straight chain, so think about surface contact.
Compare compounds 2 and 3 next, both have similar shapes but $O-H$ forms much stronger hydrogen bonds than $S-H$, so decide which must boil highest.
walkthrough:
**Sort by force type**

Think boiling point first, stronger intermolecular forces mean higher boiling point. Alkanes 1 and 4 have only weak London (induced dipole) forces, so they will boil much lower than the thiol 3 and the alcohol 2.

Order so far: alkanes < thiol, alcohol

**Compare the two alkanes**

Compound 1 is $(CH_3)_3CH$, 2-methylpropane, which is branched and almost spherical. Compound 4 is $CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_3$, n-butane, which is long and straight.

Straight chains pack closer and have more surface contact, so stronger London forces. That means 1 boils lower than 4.

**Compare thiol vs alcohol**

Compound 2 is $CH_3CH_2CH_2OH$ with an $O-H$ group. Compound 3 is $CH_3CH_2CH_2SH$ with an $S-H$ group.

Oxygen is small and very electronegative, so $O-H...O$ hydrogen bonding is strong. Sulfur is larger and much less electronegative, so $S-H$ hydrogen bonding is very weak, little stronger than dipole-dipole forces. So 3 boils lower than 2, but both boil higher than the alkanes.

$$\text{strength: London < dipole-dipole (thiol) < hydrogen bonding (alcohol)}$$

**Put the full order together**

Lowest is the branched alkane 1, then the straight alkane 4, then the thiol 3, then highest is the alcohol 2. That gives the order 1 to 4 to 3 to 2.

options.A: Incorrect. This puts 2 before 3, meaning the alcohol boils lower than the thiol. In fact $O-H$ hydrogen bonding in propan-1-ol is much stronger than the weak forces from $S-H$ in propane-1-thiol, so 2 must be highest.
options.B: Correct. Branched alkane 1 has the smallest surface area and weakest London forces, so lowest. Straight chain alkane 4 is next. Thiol 3 has polar dipole forces but only very weak H-bonding, so next. Alcohol 2 has strong $O-H$ hydrogen bonding, so highest.
options.C: Incorrect. This starts 4 to 1, meaning n-butane boils lower than branched 2-methylpropane. It is the opposite, branching reduces surface contact and London forces, so the branched isomer 1 boils lower than 4. It also swaps 2 and 3.
options.D: Incorrect. The end part 3 to 2 is correct, but the start 4 to 1 is backwards. Both are alkanes with only London forces, but the straight chain 4 has more contact area than the branched 1, so 1 is lower than 4, not higher.
